failure_summary.description: Answers were at the wrong naming granularity: too specific or formally expanded, or only a fragment of the requested compound name.
The response selected a descriptive modifier instead of the requested type of thing.
For fragmentary prompts, the agents guessed a shared category or salient associated fact without establishing the answer slot.

patch.reasoning: The most common pattern is inconsistent answer scope: agents sometimes expand a familiar short label into a formal name, but sometimes return only part of a compound name. The current naming rule can encourage over-expansion, so clarify when short forms are sufficient while retaining complete names when the requested entity is compound. The other failures are either already covered by the answer-type rules or involve ambiguous fragments for which similar broad additions have underperformed.

edits.target:
## Use the Conventional Name at the Requested Scope
For proper names and titles, use the conventional form that identifies the requested entity. Do not substitute a nickname or later brand name for the historically relevant label, omit words from a work's title when the work is requested, or add optional middle names. Conversely, when the clue requests a generic class, do not embellish it with a narrower associated name.
edits.content:
## Use the Conventional Name at the Requested Scope
For proper names and titles, use the conventional label at the scope the clue asks for; do not assume the longest formal name is required. An established short title or company label is sufficient when it uniquely identifies the target, so do not add a subtitle or corporate suffix merely because a source uses one. Conversely, when the requested answer is a compound named entity, give its complete conventional name rather than only the missing word in a cloze. Preserve historical forms and meaningful distinguishing components when the clue requires them, and do not add optional middle names. When the clue requests a generic class, do not embellish it with a narrower associated name.
